CRITICISM IN ART MEDIA
Overall: One piece found, from a culture and news outlet rather than the art press; it criticises the Gallery's public funder, not the Gallery.
1. The Spinoff: Simon Wilson, "Why is Auckland slowly strangling its art gallery?" (2017)
URL: https://thespinoff.co.nz/auckland/12-12-2017/the-gallery-of-all-our-dreams/
- Argues that Auckland Council, led by Mayor Phil Goff, underfunds the Gallery: the operating budget was NZ$6.9 million in 2017, down 25% from NZ$9.2 million in 2012, while visitors reached 550,000 against a target of 470,000.
- Says benefactor and sponsor money "doesn't keep the doors open" and opposes charging overseas visitors, who are about 60% of visitors.
- Names Goff, the director Rhana Devenport and Paul Brewer of Regional Facilities Auckland; criticises the council, not the Gallery.

BOTTOM LINE
The Gallery is publicly owned and funded through Auckland Council, with corporate partners, trusts and an endowment on top. The name to know is HSBC, a current partner whose 2012 US money-laundering settlement is documented. The public funding squeeze raised in 2017 is the other point to watch.
after:
WIDER CONTEXT
- The Spinoff, Simon Wilson, "Why is Auckland slowly strangling its art gallery?" (12 December 2017): argues that Auckland Council, led by Mayor Phil Goff, underfunds the Gallery. The Gallery's operating budget was NZ$6.9 million in the latest financial year, down 25% from NZ$9.2 million in 2012, while visitors reached 550,000 against a target of 470,000.
- Wilson writes that benefactor and sponsor money "doesn't keep the doors open", and he opposes an entry fee for overseas visitors, who are about 60% of visitors. He names Goff, the Gallery's director Rhana Devenport and Paul Brewer of Regional Facilities Auckland.
- The column's target is the council, which owns the Gallery through Tātaki Auckland Unlimited, not the Gallery itself.

BOTTOM LINE
The Gallery is publicly owned and funded through Auckland Council, with corporate partners, trusts and an endowment on top. The name to know is HSBC, a current partner that settled US money-laundering and sanctions cases in December 2012. The council's funding of the Gallery, criticised in The Spinoff in 2017, is the other point to watch.

The article gives no year for the NZ$6.9 million figure ('that same year', latest financial year), so '2017' is removed. Owned/operated by Tātaki Auckland Unlimited, a council-controlled organisation, per the Annual Review 2024/25.

meta sentence about where the findings come from
before:
- In April 2023 the Australian National Audit Office (Auditor-General Grant Hehir) concluded that the department's approach to acquiring, managing and leasing Artbank's art "has not been appropriate" (Government News, Canberra Times).
- The audit found acquisitions did not follow the Commonwealth Procurement Rules: no open or competitive process, value for money not documented, limited public reporting (Region Canberra).
- Leasing covered about 40% of the collection against a target of at least 70%; 30% of the collection was never rented from July 2015 to June 2022 and a further 29% was rented for less than half the time it was available (Canberra Times, Region Canberra).
- Approvals for over 70 works to be removed from the collection were granted retrospectively, although the works had been sold more than four years earlier (Canberra Times, Region Canberra).
- Acquisition spending fell from A$507,993 for 179 works in 2016 to 2017 to A$396,462 for 75 works in 2021 to 2022; applications to artist pitch roadshows fell from 40 in 2016 to three in 2021 (Canberra Times, Government News).
- The department's secretary, Jim Betts, said he was concerned that aspects of the audit's narrative could unduly harm Artbank's reputation, and that the department relied on a rule allowing limited tender for acquisitions (Canberra Times).
- These findings come from audit and general-press coverage, not art media. They concern Artbank's own management.
after:
- In April 2023 the Australian National Audit Office (Auditor-General Grant Hehir) found that the department's handling of Artbank "has not been appropriate" (Government News, Canberra Times).
- Acquisitions did not follow the Commonwealth Procurement Rules and skipped open or competitive processes; value for money was not documented or demonstrated, and public reporting was limited (Region Canberra, Canberra Times).
- About 40% of the collection was leased against a target of 70%; 30% was never leased from July 2015 to June 2022 and a further 29% was leased for less than half the time it was available (Government News, Region Canberra, Canberra Times).
- Approvals for removing over 70 works were obtained after the fact, though the works had been sold more than four years earlier (Region Canberra).
- Acquisition spending fell from A$507,993 for 179 works in 2016 to 2017 to A$396,462 for 75 works in 2021 to 2022; applications to the artist pitch roadshows fell from 40 in 2016 to three in 2021 (Government News).
- The department defended its approach by citing a rule allowing "limited tender". Its secretary, Jim Betts, wrote that he was "concerned that aspects of the narrative may unduly and adversely impact the reputation and operation of Artbank" (Canberra Times).
- Connection to Artbank: the audit examined Artbank's own acquisitions, leasing and records, which the department runs.
reason: Opened all three press pages (Government News 12 April 2023; Canberra Times, Natalie Vikhrov, 8 April 2023; Region Canberra, Chris Johnson, 12 April 2023). The 70% target appears in Government News and Region Canberra, not in the Canberra Times; the retroactive removal approvals and the 'more than four years' detail are in Region Canberra (the Canberra Times says the records did not show the sale); the 'limited tender' rule was cited by the department, not by Mr Betts. The line saying the findings are not from art media is meta and is cut.
